summary: Psalm 104 begins by calling the speaker’s own soul to bless Yahweh, then moves through a sweeping portrait of God clothed in light, setting earth and sea in order, watering the land, feeding animals and people, and governing day and night. The poem widens to the sea, the dependence of all creatures on God for food and breath, and ends with the speaker’s promise to sing and a wish that sinners and the wicked be gone from the earth.
whyItMatters: Inside Book IV of Psalms, this chapter is a major creation praise psalm: it places the living world, daily labor, death, renewal, and worship under God’s care and power. Its final line shows that praise and moral longing stand together in the same poem.

context.author: Anonymous; Psalms is an anthology with many writers and collections, and this chapter has no heading naming an author.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, later received by Jewish and Christian communities for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; a precise date for Psalm 104 cannot be established from this chapter alone.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, where the collection emphasizes Yahweh’s kingship, creation, and enduring rule rather than a single narrated event.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and praise, using vivid images, paired lines, and a first-person frame of blessing and song.

outline.heading: Blessing the majestic Creator
outline.note: The speaker calls his soul to bless Yahweh and pictures God clothed in honor and light, riding the clouds, and using wind and fire as messengers and servants.

outline.heading: Earth and waters set in place
outline.note: God establishes the earth, commands the waters, and sets their boundary; mountains rise and valleys sink to their assigned places.

outline.heading: Water and food for land creatures and people
outline.note: Springs, rain, grass, plants, wine, oil, bread, trees, birds, goats, and rock badgers are shown as part of God’s provision.

outline.heading: Rhythms of night, day, and work
outline.note: The moon, sun, darkness, prowling animals, lions, sunrise, dens, and human labor all have their appointed time.

outline.heading: The sea and the dependence of all life
outline.note: The poem praises the wisdom and abundance of God’s works, then says sea creatures and all living things wait on God for food, breath, death, and renewal.

outline.heading: Praise, trembling earth, and the final wish
outline.note: The speaker asks that Yahweh’s glory endure, vows lifelong song, rejoices in Yahweh, and longs for sinners and wickedness to be gone.

keyVerses.text: Bless Yahweh, my soul. Yahweh, my God, you are very great. You are clothed with honor and majesty.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm its posture: the speaker turns inward and summons his own life to praise Yahweh’s greatness.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s many images into a single claim about the abundance and wisdom of God’s works.

keyVerses.text: You hide your face; they are troubled. You take away their breath; they die and return to the dust.
keyVerses.why: The psalm’s praise includes creaturely dependence and death, not only beauty and provision.

keyVerses.text: I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live. I will sing praise to my God while I have any being.
keyVerses.why: Near the end, the speaker answers the survey of creation with a personal vow of lifelong praise.

themes: daily provision for animals and people
ordered rhythms of night and day
creaturely dependence on breath and food
praise joined to longing for wickedness to end

questions.question: What kind of psalm is Psalm 104?
questions.answer: It is a praise poem centered on God as creator and sustainer. The chapter does not narrate a single event; it moves through images of sky, earth, water, plants, animals, people, sea, life, death, renewal, and worship.

questions.question: Why does the speaker say, “Bless Yahweh, my soul”?
questions.answer: The speaker is addressing himself and calling his own life to praise. The same phrase returns at the end, so the whole poem is framed as self-summoned worship rather than detached observation.

questions.question: Is the poem describing creation in the same way as a history report?
questions.answer: Psalm 104 is poetry, not a step-by-step prose account. It uses images such as light as a garment, heavens like a curtain, clouds as a chariot, and waters fleeing at God’s rebuke to praise God’s rule over the ordered world.

questions.question: What is the point of the water imagery?
questions.answer: Water appears first as something God restrains and then as something God gives. The waters are assigned boundaries, but springs and rain also sustain animals, trees, crops, and people.

questions.question: Why are so many animals named?
questions.answer: The chapter pictures creation as a shared world in which wild donkeys, birds, storks, wild goats, rock badgers, lions, sea creatures, and leviathan all have places and needs. Human life is included, but it is not the only life God provides for.

questions.question: What is “leviathan” doing here?
questions.answer: The verse says leviathan is in the sea and that God formed it “to play there.” Readers differ on how to relate this image to other biblical uses of leviathan, but in this chapter the creature belongs within God’s made world rather than outside God’s control.

questions.question: Does the psalm treat death as outside God’s world?
questions.answer: No. The poem says living things are troubled when God hides his face, and when God takes away their breath they die and return to dust. It then speaks of God sending Spirit and renewing the ground, so mortality and renewal both appear inside the chapter’s praise.

questions.question: Why does a praise psalm end by asking that sinners be consumed?
questions.answer: The final wish is jarring because most of the chapter has been celebrating life and provision. The verse shows that the speaker’s praise also includes a desire for wickedness to disappear from the earth; readers differ on how to pray such lines today, but the chapter itself places that longing beside “Bless Yahweh, my soul.”

questions.question: What does “Praise Yah” mean at the end?
questions.answer: The Hebrew form means “praise Yah,” a plural command using a shortened form of the divine name. In the chapter, it comes after the speaker has already called his own soul to bless Yahweh, so the ending widens the call to praise.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this translation of the psalm. The chapter addresses Yahweh as creator, provider, ruler, and the one the speaker praises.
The speaker’s own living self, addressed at the beginning and end with the command to bless Yahweh.
A sea creature named in verse 26. In this chapter it is pictured in the wide sea as something God formed to play there.
What God sends out in verse 30, after the poem has spoken of breath, death, and return to dust. The line connects God’s action with creation and renewal.
